questions.stem: From which Greek verb is the word 'drama' derived, and what does it mean?

options.A: 'Dran' meaning 'to act or perform'
options.B: 'Drao' meaning 'to write'
options.C: 'Drama' meaning 'to imitate'
options.D: 'Dromos' meaning 'a race'

questions.explanation: Drama is derived from the Greek verb 'dran' which means 'to act or perform'.

questions.stem: Drama is used at three different levels. Which of the following correctly lists them?

options.A: Performance, Composition, Branch of Literature
options.B: Tragedy, Comedy, Tragicomedy
options.C: Plot, Setting, Theme
options.D: Action, Dialogue, Conflict

questions.explanation: Drama is used at three levels: as performance (acted on stage/screen), as composition (a written piece using language and dialogue), and as a branch of literature distinct from prose and poetry.

questions.stem: Why is drama as a performance considered different from a musical performance?

options.A: Drama is performed by actors and actresses telling stories with other characters, unlike a solo musical act
options.B: Drama does not require a stage
options.C: Drama has no audience
options.D: Drama cannot be acted on screen

questions.explanation: As performance, drama is used for plays acted on stage or screen; this differs from musical performance because drama tells stories acted out by actors and actresses interacting with other characters.

questions.stem: At the level of composition, drama makes use of which key element to present a story or event to be performed?

options.A: Language and stage movement/dramatic performance of the body
options.B: Only narration
options.C: Only rhyme
options.D: Only stanza form

questions.explanation: As a composition, drama uses language and the dramatic performance/movement of the body to present a story or event meant to be performed.

questions.stem: What is the major difference between drama and other forms of literature (prose and poetry)?

options.A: Drama makes use of dialogue from beginning to end and information is passed on a stage
options.B: Drama does not have characters
options.C: Drama is always shorter than prose
options.D: Drama cannot be read, only watched

questions.explanation: The major difference between drama and other forms of literature is that drama makes use of dialogue from the beginning to the end, and information is passed on a stage.

questions.stem: Unlike poems which are written in stanzas, how is drama typically presented?

options.A: In acts and scenes
options.B: In chapters and verses
options.C: In paragraphs only
options.D: In footnotes

questions.explanation: In chapters, a poem is written in stanzas, but drama is presented in acts and scenes; William Shakespeare made the five-act structure the standard for his plays.

questions.stem: Why is drama considered unique in nature compared to prose and poetry?

options.A: Because it can be both read and performed, unlike prose and poetry which are basically narrations
options.B: Because it has no plot
options.C: Because it cannot be written down
options.D: Because it does not require characters

questions.explanation: Drama is unique because it can be read and also be performed, unlike prose and poetry which are basically narrations and drama is presented only through dialogue.

questions.stem: What does 'imitation' mean in the context of drama?

options.A: A reflection of an action in real life although close to reality but not reality
options.B: An exact duplication of real events with no illusion
options.C: Copying somebody's personality completely and permanently
options.D: A scene that never relates to real life

questions.explanation: Imitation is a reflection of an action in real life; although it is close to reality, it is not reality itself. In imitation, you take the personality of the person you are imitating and an illusion of reality is created to make the action seem real or credible.

questions.stem: How does 'impersonation' differ from imitation in drama?

options.A: Impersonation is copying people, while imitation is copying something; actors must be able to convince the audience that they are the characters they are impersonating
options.B: Impersonation only happens in comedy
options.C: Impersonation means writing a script
options.D: Impersonation and imitation mean exactly the same thing

questions.explanation: Imitation is copying somebody or something, but impersonation is specifically copying people; the actors must convince the audience that they are the characters they are impersonating.

questions.stem: In the context of origins/definitions of drama, what does 're-presentation' mean?

options.A: To show something again
options.B: To delete a previous performance
options.C: To write a new play
options.D: To translate a play into another language

questions.explanation: Re-presentation refers to showing something again, while re-enactment refers to actors or characters who impersonate specific characters in the main action.

questions.stem: According to the Ritual Origin Theory, what triggered the act of appeasing the gods through rituals?

options.A: When there was chaos or when the land was not yielding fruit, people thought they had offended the gods
options.B: When kings wanted entertainment
options.C: When playwrights wanted to make money
options.D: When actors wanted costumes

questions.explanation: Many scholars argue drama emanated from ritual. When there was chaos or when the land was not yielding fruit, people believed they had offended the gods, and the act of appeasing the gods was called a ritual.

questions.stem: Who performed the ritual in the origin-of-drama account, and what did this person do?

options.A: A priest in a shrine, who wore a special dress (costume) and made some incantations or utterances
options.B: A king, who simply prayed silently
options.C: A child, who sang songs
options.D: A merchant, who sold goods

questions.explanation: The ritual was performed by a priest in a shrine; the priest would wear a special dress (costume) and make some incantations or utterances.

questions.stem: Aside from ritual, what other account explains the origin of drama?

options.A: Man's desire for entertainment, where during festivals people re-created mythical heroes or legends
options.B: The invention of the printing press
options.C: The need for written law codes
options.D: The construction of amphitheaters

questions.explanation: Another account of the origin of drama is man's desire for entertainment; during festivals or other ceremonies, people recreated mythical heroes or legendary figures to entertain the people.

questions.stem: Why is the origin of drama traced more popularly to Greece rather than Egypt, even though some say it evolved from Egypt?

options.A: Because Greece's origin of drama is more documented
options.B: Because Egypt had no civilization
options.C: Because Greek plays were shorter
options.D: Because Egypt did not have festivals

questions.explanation: Some scholars trace the origin of drama to Egypt, reportedly one of the cradles of civilization, but tracing the origin to Greece is more popular because it is more documented.

questions.stem: Greek drama started from religious festivals (rituals) held in honour of which god, and why?

options.A: Dionysus, the native god who dies and is reborn each year, to ensure the well-being of the people and fertility of the land
options.B: Zeus, the king of all gods
options.C: Apollo, the god of the sun
options.D: Poseidon, the god of the sea

questions.explanation: Greek drama started from religious festivals (rituals) done to ensure the well-being of the people and the fertility of the land. These festivals were in worship of the god Dionysus, a native god who dies and is reborn each year.

questions.stem: What was the choral song sung in honour of Dionysus during the festival called, and who performed it?

options.A: Dithyramb, sung by a chorus of fifty men
options.B: Sonnet, sung by a single priest
options.C: Anthem, sung by women only
options.D: Hymn, sung by children

questions.explanation: During the festival, singing and dancing were done by a chorus of fifty men singing in honour of the god; the choral song is known as Dithyramb, performed around the altar of Dionysus in a dancing place called Orchestra.

questions.stem: Who is believed to have been the first actor to introduce the individual actor and the element of impersonation in the 6th century BC?

options.A: Thespis
options.B: Aeschylus
options.C: Sophocles
options.D: Aristotle

questions.explanation: Thespis is believed to have been the first actor/person to introduce the individual actor and the element of impersonation in the 6th century BC, by pretending to be the god instead of merely singing in his honour, thereby adding the dramatic potential of impersonation.

questions.stem: Who became the second actor in Greek drama, and who became the third, changing the performance to drama?

options.A: Aeschylus became the second actor, and Sophocles became the third
options.B: Sophocles became the second actor, and Aeschylus became the third
options.C: Aristotle became the second actor, and Plato became the third
options.D: Thespis became the second actor, and Homer became the third

questions.explanation: Aeschylus became the second actor, then Sophocles became the third actor, so performance changed from poetry performance to drama.

questions.stem: What does the Mimetic Impulse Theory of the origin of drama propose?

options.A: Drama originated from the imitation of actions (the imitation of actions)
options.B: Drama originated from written law books
options.C: Drama originated from mathematics
options.D: Drama originated from agricultural tools

questions.explanation: The Mimetic Impulse Theory holds that the origin of drama lies in the imitation of actions - humans' natural impulse to imitate or mimic actions and behaviours.

questions.stem: What are the three main components of drama as identified in the notes?

options.A: Action, Dialogue, and Conflict
options.B: Plot, Setting, and Theme
options.C: Tragedy, Comedy, and Tragicomedy
options.D: Prologue, Epilogue, and Climax

questions.explanation: The components of drama are Action, Dialogue, and Conflict.

questions.stem: How is 'Action' described as a component of drama?

options.A: The play emerges from the enactment of action before an audience, and it is what keeps the plot moving
options.B: It is the verbal exchange among characters
options.C: It is the struggle for supremacy between protagonist and antagonist
options.D: It is the central message of the play

questions.explanation: Action is the component through which the play emerges from the enactment of action before an audience, and it is what keeps the plot moving.

questions.stem: As a component of drama, conflict is described as what kind of force?

options.A: A continuing force in a drama which comes naturally out of the interaction of the characters
options.B: A force that only appears in tragedies
options.C: A force created solely by the audience
options.D: A force that has no relation to characters

questions.explanation: As a component, conflict is a continuing force in a drama which comes naturally out of the interaction of the characters; it always manifests when the play reaches the climax and is resolved at the end, known as denouement.

questions.stem: What is dialogue, and what is the one technique that does NOT make use of dialogue?

options.A: Dialogue is the verbal exchange among characters that releases the playwright's intentions; Mime does not make use of dialogue
options.B: Dialogue is stage direction; Soliloquy does not use dialogue
options.C: Dialogue is the setting; Flashback does not use dialogue
options.D: Dialogue is costume description; Suspense does not use dialogue

questions.explanation: Dialogue is the verbal exchange among characters which helps to release the intention of the playwright, except for Mime, which does not make use of dialogue.

questions.stem: Conflict, as a feature of drama, is best described as:

options.A: A struggle for supremacy between the protagonist and antagonist of the play, usually resolved at the end
options.B: A song sung by a chorus
options.C: The opening speech of a play
options.D: A scene depicting only comic relief

questions.explanation: Conflict is a struggle for supremacy between the protagonist and antagonist of the play. The conflict is usually resolved, and this is referred to as conflict resolution or denouement.

questions.stem: Which definition best matches 'plot' as a feature/element of drama?

options.A: The central plan of events in a play that runs from the beginning to the end
options.B: An introductory address before a play begins
options.C: A short scene at the end of a play
options.D: The location where a play is set

questions.explanation: Plot is the central plan of events in a play that runs from the beginning to the end.

questions.stem: What is a 'scene' in drama, and how does it relate to an act?

options.A: The performable parts into which a drama is divided; scenes are under an act, and a play made up of acts is itself made up of scenes
options.B: The introductory speech before a play
options.C: The final speech that closes a play
options.D: Only the costume changes between acts

questions.explanation: Scenes are the performable parts into which a drama is divided. Scenes are under an act, and they are a complete episode to be dramatized; a play is made up of acts, and acts are made up of scenes.

questions.stem: What is a prologue?

options.A: An introductory scene, address, or speech made before the commencement of a play
options.B: A short scene at the end of a play
options.C: A struggle between two characters
options.D: The climax of a play

questions.explanation: A prologue is an introductory scene or address/speech made before the commencement of a play.

questions.stem: How does an epilogue relate to a prologue?

options.A: An epilogue is the opposite of a prologue: a short scene/speech at the end of a play used in closing
options.B: An epilogue and a prologue mean the same thing
options.C: An epilogue always comes before the prologue
options.D: An epilogue is a type of conflict

questions.explanation: An epilogue is the opposite of a prologue; it is a short scene at the end of a play, a final speech or address used in closing a play.

questions.stem: Apart from conflict, plot, scenes, prologue and epilogue, which of the following is also listed as another feature of drama?

options.A: Flashback, suspense, climax, interlude, cast, dramatis personae, and soliloquy
options.B: Photosynthesis
options.C: Stanza and rhyme scheme
options.D: Footnotes and bibliography

questions.explanation: Other features of drama listed include flashback, suspense, climax, interlude, cast, dramatis personae, and soliloquy.

questions.stem: Which set correctly lists the elements of drama as covered in this course?

options.A: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Character
options.B: Suspense, Comic relief, Flashback, and Foreshadowing
options.C: Tragedy, Comedy, and Tragicomedy
options.D: Prologue and Epilogue only

questions.explanation: The elements of drama covered are Plot (a sequential arrangement of events, the story a play tells), Setting (the location of the literary work), Theme (the central message of a play), and Character (people who are allotted roles in a play).

questions.stem: As an element of drama, plot is defined as:

options.A: A sequential arrangement of events; it is the story that a play tells
options.B: The location of the literary work
options.C: The central message of a play
options.D: People who are allotted roles in a play

questions.explanation: Plot is a sequential arrangement of events; it is the story a play tells.

questions.stem: What does 'setting' refer to in a play?

options.A: The location of the literary work
options.B: The struggle between characters
options.C: The introduction of characters
options.D: The height of conflict

questions.explanation: Setting refers to the location of the literary work.

questions.stem: What is the 'theme' of a play?

options.A: The central message of a play
options.B: The actors in the play
options.C: The opening scene of the play
options.D: The setting of the play

questions.explanation: Theme refers to the central message of a play.

questions.stem: Which five elements are described as important to the plot of a play?

options.A: Exposition, Complication, Climax, Denouement, and Resolution/Conclusion
options.B: Plot, Setting, Theme, Character, and Conflict
options.C: Tragedy, Comedy, Suspense, Irony, and Catharsis
options.D: Prologue, Epilogue, Scene, Act, and Cast

questions.explanation: The five elements important to the plot of a play are Exposition, Complication, Climax, and after climax, Denouement (which also means resolution or conclusion).

questions.stem: What happens during the 'Exposition' stage of a play's plot?

options.A: Introduction of the characters in a play
options.B: The height of conflict in the play
options.C: An obstacle placed in the protagonist's way
options.D: The untying of the knot at the play's end

questions.explanation: Exposition is the introduction of the characters in a play.

questions.stem: What is 'Complication' in the structure of a play's plot?

options.A: An obstacle on the way of the protagonist
options.B: The introduction of characters
options.C: The untying of a knot
options.D: A speech at the close of a play

questions.explanation: Complication is an obstacle on the way of the protagonist.

questions.stem: What occurs at the 'Climax' of a play?

options.A: The height of conflict in the play, where there will be a major place that leads to resolution of the major problem
options.B: The introduction of all characters
options.C: The untying of a knot in French terms
options.D: An obstacle in the protagonist's path

questions.explanation: Climax is the height of conflict in the play; at this level there will be a major place/event that will lead to the resolution of the major problem in the play.

questions.stem: What does 'Denouement' mean, and what French phrase does it derive from?

options.A: It means 'untying of a knot' in French, and also means resolution or conclusion
options.B: It means 'tying of a knot' in French, and means the introduction of characters
options.C: It means 'beginning of conflict' in Latin
options.D: It means 'climax' in Greek

questions.explanation: Denouement, which comes after climax, in French means 'untying of a knot'. It also means resolution or conclusion.

questions.stem: How are 'Characters' defined in drama?

options.A: Persons, animals, or things created by the playwright to act or play in a drama
options.B: The events that make up the plot
options.C: The location of the play
options.D: The central message conveyed by the play

questions.explanation: Characters are persons, animals, or things created by the playwright to act or play a drama.

questions.stem: What is a 'Flat Character'?

options.A: A static character who does not change from the beginning of the play to the end
options.B: A character who grows and develops with the play
options.C: The leading character of the play
options.D: The character whose aim is to contend with the protagonist

questions.explanation: A flat character is a static character; they do not change from the beginning of the play to the end.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a 'Round Character' from a flat character?

options.A: Round characters are dynamic; they grow and develop with the play, and are usually the main characters
options.B: Round characters never change
options.C: Round characters always die at the end of the play
options.D: Round characters never speak

questions.explanation: Round characters are dynamic; they grow and develop with the play, and they are usually the main characters.

questions.stem: Who is the 'Protagonist' of a play?

options.A: The leading character in a play, around whom the entire action of the play centres; the hero or heroine
options.B: The villain who opposes the hero
options.C: A minor character with no impact on the plot
options.D: The author of the play

questions.explanation: Protagonist is the leading character in a play; the entire action of the play centres on him/her, as they are the hero or heroine of the play.

questions.stem: What is the main aim of the 'Antagonist' in a play?

options.A: To contend with the protagonist; antagonists are always against the protagonist and always lead to the protagonist's downfall
options.B: To support and protect the protagonist
options.C: To introduce all the characters
options.D: To narrate the play's events

questions.explanation: The main aim of the antagonist is to contend with the protagonist; they are always against the protagonist and always lead to the downfall of the protagonist.

questions.stem: Who is a 'Playwright'?

options.A: The author/writer of a drama text or play
options.B: The person who directs the actors on stage
options.C: The character that opposes the protagonist
options.D: The person who designs costumes

questions.explanation: A playwright is the author or writer of a drama text or play.

questions.stem: What is 'Suspense' as a dramatic technique?

options.A: A common strategy used by playwrights to keep the reader or audience in anxious expectation of what will happen next in the play
options.B: Light or unserious action marked by laughter
options.C: Bringing in a supernatural force to solve a problem
options.D: A detachment effected by directors so the audience does not get too emotionally involved

questions.explanation: Suspense is a common strategy in drama used by playwrights to keep the reader or audience in anxious expectation of what will happen next in the play.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of 'Comic Relief' in a play?

options.A: To create some atmosphere of relief after serious or tragic action, making the audience laugh and getting rid of tension created by serious action
options.B: To introduce all the characters at the start of the play
options.C: To bring a supernatural force on stage
options.D: To show a past event in the present

questions.explanation: Comic relief is light or unserious action marked by laughter after some serious or tragic action; it creates an atmosphere of relief in a play, often done by clowns, with the aim of making the audience laugh and getting rid of tension created earlier by serious action.

questions.stem: What does 'Flashback' enable a playwright to do?

options.A: Bring a past experience to the present in order to understand a particular matter
options.B: Show an experience in the future
options.C: Bring a supernatural force to solve a problem on stage
options.D: Detach the audience emotionally from the play

questions.explanation: Flashback enables the playwright to bring a past experience to the present in order to understand a particular matter.

questions.stem: What is the function of 'Foreshadowing' as a dramatic technique?

options.A: It enables a playwright to give an experience in the future, creating anxiety and anticipation of the experience
options.B: It enables a playwright to bring a past event into the present
options.C: It is used to create laughter after a tragic scene
options.D: It introduces a supernatural force into the play

questions.explanation: Foreshadowing enables a playwright to give an experience in the future; it creates anxiety and anticipation of the experience.

questions.stem: When does 'Dramatic Irony' occur in a play?

options.A: When an event or situation is seen in a particular way by a character in a play, whereas the audience and some other characters have a proper outlook on it
options.B: When a supernatural being solves a problem on stage
options.C: When a play has no conflict
options.D: When the audience laughs at a serious scene

questions.explanation: Dramatic irony happens when an event or situation is seen in a particular way by a character in a play, whereas the audience and some other characters have a proper (more accurate) outlook on it.

questions.stem: What does 'Deus Ex Machina' mean as a dramatic device?

options.A: Bringing in a supernatural force (a god) to the stage to solve a problem
options.B: Bringing a past experience to the present
options.C: Creating laughter after a serious scene
options.D: Making the audience anxious about the future

questions.explanation: Deus Ex Machina means bringing in a supernatural force (a god) to the stage to solve a problem.

questions.stem: What is the 'Alienation Effect', and why is it used by directors?

options.A: A detachment injected by directors into the way actors and audience relate with their plays, to prevent too much emotional involvement
options.B: A technique to make the audience cry uncontrollably
options.C: A method of bringing a god onto the stage
options.D: A method of introducing flashbacks

questions.explanation: Alienation Effect is a detachment injected by directors into the way actors and audience relate with their plays; it is used to prevent too much emotional involvement.

questions.stem: From which Greek words is 'Tragedy' derived, and what do they mean?

options.A: 'Tragos' (goat) and 'ode' (song)
options.B: 'Komos' (revel) and 'logos' (word)
options.C: 'Mimesis' (imitation) and 'graphe' (writing)
options.D: 'Pathos' (suffering) and 'ethos' (character)

questions.explanation: Tragedy comes from the Greek words 'tragos' (goat) and 'ode' (song); tragedy can be traced to Greece in the 5th century BC.

questions.stem: According to Aristotle, tragedy is the representation of an action that is:

options.A: Serious, complete in itself, and of a certain amplitude, presented through action (not narration), bringing about a purgation (catharsis) of emotion
options.B: Comic, incomplete, and short in length, narrated by a single speaker
options.C: Random, fragmented, and lacking any plot structure
options.D: Only meant to be read silently, never performed

questions.explanation: To Aristotle, tragedy is a representation of an action that is worth serious attention, complete in itself, and of a certain amplitude, enriched by a variety of artistic devices appropriate to the parts of a play, presented in the form of action, not narration, and bringing about a purgation of emotion (catharsis) through pity and fear.

questions.stem: In classical (Aristotelian) tragedy, what is required of the tragic hero?

options.A: The hero must be a noble man, as the fall of an ordinary man cannot provoke dramatic interest; the hero must be a king or highly placed person
options.B: The hero must always be a commoner so the audience can relate
options.C: The hero must never face any conflict
options.D: The hero must be comic in nature

questions.explanation: In classical tragedy, the tragic hero is expected to be a noble man, because the fall of an ordinary man cannot be considered to provoke dramatic interest. The tragic hero must either be a king or a highly placed person.

questions.stem: Why is elevated language (verse) considered the ideal language for classical tragedy?

options.A: Because only elevated language would be suitable for the class of people that were the object of tragedy
options.B: Because verse is easier to memorize than prose
options.C: Because elevated language makes the play shorter
options.D: Because the audience could not understand prose

questions.explanation: Elevated language is seen as the ideal language for tragedy in the classical tradition because only elevated language would be suitable for the class of people that were the object of tragedy.

questions.stem: What are the 'Three Unities' in classical tragedy?

options.A: Unity of Time, Place, and Action
options.B: Unity of Plot, Theme, and Setting
options.C: Unity of Conflict, Climax, and Denouement
options.D: Unity of Comedy, Tragedy, and Tragicomedy

questions.explanation: The Three Unities are Time, Place, and Action.

questions.stem: What does the 'Unity of Time' require in classical tragedy?

options.A: The action of a play must not go beyond a day
options.B: The action must happen in a single locale
options.C: Only one action should be seen on stage at any time
options.D: The play must last exactly one hour

questions.explanation: The Unity of Time means the action of a play must not go beyond a day.

questions.stem: What does the 'Unity of Place' require?

options.A: The action must happen in a locale (one place)
options.B: The action must happen across multiple countries
options.C: There must be no setting at all
options.D: The action must happen in the future

questions.explanation: The Unity of Place means the action must happen in a locale, i.e., one place.

questions.stem: What does the 'Unity of Action' require, and what does it rule out?

options.A: Only one action should be seen on stage at any time, and the plot must be tight with no room for comic relief
options.B: Multiple unrelated plots should run simultaneously
options.C: The play must include several subplots and comic relief
options.D: Time must be unrestricted

questions.explanation: Unity of Action means only one action should be seen on the stage at any time; the plot must be tight, and there should be no room for comic relief.

questions.stem: What is 'Hubris' in classical tragedy?

options.A: The hero's tragic flaw - a weakness in his character which would lead to his fall
options.B: The purgation of emotions
options.C: A type of comic relief
options.D: A supernatural intervention

questions.explanation: Hubris is the hero's tragic flaw or tragic flow; Aristotle expects the tragic hero to have a weakness in his character which would lead to his fall.

questions.stem: What is 'Catharsis' in classical tragedy, and what does it relate to?

options.A: Purgation of emotions; it relates directly to the effect of the hero's fall on the audience
options.B: The introduction of characters at the start of a play
options.C: A comic technique to relieve tension
options.D: A supernatural force solving a problem

questions.explanation: Catharsis is the purgation of emotions; it relates directly to the effect of the fall of the hero on the audience. The fall of the tragic hero is meant to elicit the purgation of emotion due to the relief that the hero's fall will cause.

questions.stem: In which Sophoclean play's classical tragedy example does the hero suffer for sleeping with his mother and killing his father?

options.A: Oedipus (referenced as the example in Sophocles)
options.B: Antigone
options.C: Electra
options.D: Ajax

questions.explanation: In the example given from Sophocles, the hero is supposed to die for sleeping with his mother and killing his father - this is the story of Oedipus.

questions.stem: Which dates are given for William Shakespeare in the notes, and what did he do with the principles of classical tragedy?

options.A: 1564-1616; he upheld many principles of classical tragedy but disregarded a few, such as the social status requirement for the hero
options.B: 1700-1750; he invented the unities entirely
options.C: 1450-1500; he abolished tragedy as a form
options.D: 1800-1850; he wrote only comedies

questions.explanation: William Shakespeare (1564-1616) upheld many of the principles of classical tragedy but disregarded a few; for Shakespeare, the social status of the hero is not important, though the hero must still be highly placed (king, prince, war general, distinguished member of society, not a commoner).

questions.stem: Which of the following is listed among Shakespeare's main tragedies in the notes?

options.A: Julius Caesar, Hamlet, Othello, Macbeth, King Lear, and Antony and Cleopatra
options.B: A Midsummer Night's Dream
options.C: Twelfth Night
options.D: The Tempest

questions.explanation: Shakespeare's main tragedies listed include Julius Caesar, Hamlet, Othello, Macbeth, King Lear, and Antony and Cleopatra.

questions.stem: What is 'Tragic-Comedy' (tragicomedy)?

options.A: It blends the attributes of both tragedy and comedy; it has both tragic and comic feelings with two emerging plots
options.B: It is pure tragedy with no comic elements
options.C: It is pure comedy with no tragic elements
options.D: It only occurs in modern drama, never in classical drama

questions.explanation: Tragic-comedy blends the attributes of both tragedy and comedy; it has both tragic and comic feelings with two emerging plots.

questions.stem: Which examples are given of Shakespearean heroes whose hubris leads to their tragic fall?

options.A: Othello, seen as jealous and gullible; he makes use of elevated language and deviates from the unities of time, place, and action
options.B: Hamlet, seen as cowardly and silent throughout the play
options.C: Macbeth, seen as entirely innocent of any flaw
options.D: King Lear, who has no character flaws at all

questions.explanation: In Shakespearean tragedies, the element of hubris (the hero's weakness that always leads to the tragic fall) is always present; e.g., Othello is seen as jealous and gullible. Shakespeare's heroes make use of elevated language and deviate from the idea of unities of time, place, and action.

questions.stem: How does Modern Tragedy depart from classical tragedy, according to the notes?

options.A: Not only the noble or highly placed can be a subject of tragedy; the ordinary man can also be a subject of tragedy
options.B: Modern tragedy requires the hero to be a king
options.C: Modern tragedy removed catharsis entirely
options.D: Modern tragedy no longer has any conflict

questions.explanation: Modern Tragedy is a departure from classical tragedy; it asserts that not only the noble or the highly placed could be a subject of tragedy, but the ordinary man could also be a subject of tragedy. This is seen in the works of Arthur Miller and Henrik Ibsen.

questions.stem: Which play is given as an example of Modern Tragedy, and who wrote it?

options.A: 'Death of a Salesman' by Arthur Miller, whose tragic hero (Willy Loman) is not a noble man or of high birth
options.B: 'Hamlet' by William Shakespeare, whose hero is a prince
options.C: 'Oedipus Rex' by Sophocles, whose hero is a king
options.D: 'Antigone' by Sophocles, whose heroine is a princess

questions.explanation: The example given of Modern Tragedy is 'Death of a Salesman' by American playwright Arthur Miller; the tragic hero, Willy Loman, is not a noble man or of high birth.

questions.stem: In Modern Tragedy, how are Aristotle's requirements for tragedy treated?

options.A: All the requirements made by Aristotle are disregarded
options.B: All the requirements made by Aristotle are strictly followed
options.C: Only the unity of time is disregarded; all others are kept
options.D: Aristotle's requirements are doubled in number

questions.explanation: In Modern Tragedy, all the requirements made by Aristotle are disregarded.

questions.stem: From which Greek word is 'Comedy' derived, and what does it mean?

options.A: 'Komos', meaning 'revel'
options.B: 'Tragos', meaning 'goat'
options.C: 'Mimesis', meaning 'imitation'
options.D: 'Pathos', meaning 'suffering'

questions.explanation: Comedy is from the Greek word 'Komos' which means 'revel'. It also originated from ritual performance in honour of the Greek god of fertility and wine called Dionysus.

questions.stem: How does comedy differ from tragedy in terms of audience appeal, according to the notes?

options.A: Tragedy appeals to our emotion, while comedy appeals to our reason; comedy makes us think due to the issues it raises
options.B: Comedy appeals to our emotion, while tragedy appeals to our reason
options.C: Both comedy and tragedy appeal only to emotion
options.D: Neither comedy nor tragedy appeals to emotion or reason

questions.explanation: Comedy is the opposite of tragedy; tragedy appeals to our emotion while comedy appeals to our reason. Comedy makes us think due to the issues it raises.

questions.stem: What was Aristotle's view of comedy's importance compared to tragedy?

options.A: To Aristotle, comedy detracts from the importance of its subject and is therefore inferior
options.B: To Aristotle, comedy is superior to tragedy
options.C: To Aristotle, comedy and tragedy are equally important
options.D: Aristotle did not have any opinion on comedy

questions.explanation: Comedy originated from Greece; to Aristotle, it detracts from the importance of its subject, and therefore it is inferior.

questions.stem: According to the notes, comedy is a medium for what purpose?

options.A: The correction of social ills
options.B: The glorification of kings
options.C: The destruction of moral values
options.D: The promotion of war

questions.explanation: Comedy is a medium for the correction of social ills.

questions.stem: Which two broad forms of comedy are identified in the notes?

options.A: High comedy and Low comedy
options.B: Classical comedy and Modern comedy
options.C: Verbal comedy and Physical comedy
options.D: Greek comedy and Roman comedy

questions.explanation: The forms of comedy are High comedy and Low comedy, which are also referred to as 'comedy of situations' and 'comedy of manners'.

questions.stem: What characterizes 'High Comedy'?

options.A: It elicits a form of laughter that is thoughtful; when trying to correct man, it is friendly
options.B: It is unsparing in ridiculing man
options.C: It uses only slapstick and farce
options.D: It never raises any social issue

questions.explanation: High comedy elicits a form of laughter that is thoughtful; when trying to correct man, it is friendly.

questions.stem: What characterizes 'Low Comedy', and what are its examples?

options.A: It is unsparing in ridiculing man; it is reflected in the form of laughter it provokes - examples are slapstick, farce, and marionette
options.B: It is gentle and reflective; examples are tragedy and elegy
options.C: It always corrects social ills in a friendly manner
options.D: It has no examples in drama

questions.explanation: Low comedy is unsparing in ridiculing man; it is reflected in the form of laughter it provokes. Examples are slapstick, farce, and marionette.

questions.stem: Which of the following is listed as a function of drama?

options.A: It entertains, informs, and educates people
options.B: It only entertains and has no other purpose
options.C: It is only useful for religious worship
options.D: It cannot present a story realistically

questions.explanation: One of the functions of drama is that it entertains, informs, and educates people.

questions.stem: How does drama present a story to the audience, according to the listed functions?

options.A: It presents a story in a realistic fashion through the actors to the audience
options.B: It presents a story only through narration
options.C: It presents a story only in written form, never performed
options.D: It presents a story only as statistics

questions.explanation: Drama presents a story in a realistic fashion through the actors to the audience.

questions.stem: Drama is described as an effective tool for what kind of social purpose?

options.A: Mass mobilization
options.B: Tax collection
options.C: Currency exchange
options.D: Weather forecasting

questions.explanation: Drama is an effective tool for mass mobilization.

questions.stem: Which two functions are described together regarding the immediacy of drama's message and its role in society?

options.A: Its message is immediate, and it forms part of communal rites
options.B: Its message takes years to reach people, and it has no link to communal life
options.C: It cannot mirror society in any way
options.D: It only exists in written form and never affects communities

questions.explanation: Among drama's functions: its message is immediate, and it forms part of communal rites.

questions.stem: How does drama relate to society, according to its functions?

options.A: It mirrors society and helps to effect social reforms
options.B: It has no relationship with society
options.C: It only entertains the wealthy
options.D: It always supports the status quo with no possibility of reform

questions.explanation: Drama mirrors the society and helps to effect social reforms.

questions.stem: According to the discussion questions in the notes, who can enjoy and assimilate the message of drama, provided it is presented in the appropriate language?

options.A: Both the rich and the poor, the young and old, the literate and illiterate
options.B: Only highly educated people
options.C: Only the wealthy upper class
options.D: Only children

questions.explanation: Both the rich and the poor, the young and old, the literate and illiterate enjoy and assimilate the message of drama if it is presented in the appropriate language.

questions.stem: Besides entertaining, what else does drama do regarding life's problems, according to the discussion notes?

options.A: It treats life's basic problems and also attacks social ills
options.B: It avoids discussing any real-life problems
options.C: It only discusses fictional, fantastical worlds
options.D: It ignores social issues entirely

questions.explanation: Drama treats life's basic problems and also attacks social ills.

questions.stem: How was drama used during the Medieval period?

options.A: It was used to preach the gospel through the re-enactment of biblical stories during mass, for spiritual and moral growth of the people
options.B: It was banned entirely by the church
options.C: It was used solely for military training
options.D: It was used only for royal entertainment with no religious purpose

questions.explanation: During the Medieval period, drama was used to preach the gospel through the re-enactment of biblical stories during mass; it was used for the spiritual and moral growth of the people.

questions.stem: Which playwrights are named as examples from England, France, and Germany who used drama for such purposes?

options.A: Shakespeare, Goethe, Brecht, and Molière
options.B: Homer, Virgil, and Dante
options.C: Chaucer, Milton, and Spenser
options.D: Ibsen, Strindberg, and Chekhov

questions.explanation: In England, France, and Germany, playwrights like Shakespeare, Goethe, Brecht, and Molière used drama through their works for these purposes.

questions.stem: According to Ahaher (45) as cited in the notes, what do dramatic works carve out and affirm?

options.A: A unique identity for themselves
options.B: A universal language understood by all
options.C: A fixed set of unchanging morals
options.D: A new alphabet system

questions.explanation: Dramatic works carve out and affirm a unique identity for themselves (Ahaher 45).

questions.stem: Which examples are given of plays that caused social or political reactions, according to the notes?

options.A: Arthur Miller's 'Death of a Salesman' aroused industrial revolution awareness in America, and Ngugi wa Thiong'o was arrested because of his play 'I Will Marry When I Want' in Kenya
options.B: Shakespeare's 'Hamlet' caused a revolution in Denmark
options.C: Sophocles' 'Oedipus' caused riots in Athens
options.D: Molière's plays caused a war in France

questions.explanation: Arthur Miller's 'Death of a Salesman' caused/aroused industrial revolution consciousness in America; in Kenya, Ngugi wa Thiong'o was arrested because of his play 'I Will Marry When I Want' due to the political and social consciousness of the play.

questions.stem: How does drama reflect the cultural background of a people, according to the notes?

options.A: Through the use of myths, music, dance, songs, proverbs, riddles, and other local expressions
options.B: Only through written text with no performance elements
options.C: Only through foreign languages
options.D: Only through silence and mime

questions.explanation: Drama reflects the cultural background of the people through the use of myths, music, dance, songs, proverbs, riddles, and other local expressions.

questions.stem: According to the notes, dramatists can be regarded as custodians of what?

options.A: Cultural and moral values
options.B: National currencies
options.C: Scientific formulas
options.D: Legal statutes

questions.explanation: Dramatists can be regarded as custodians of cultural and moral values.

questions.stem: According to the LIT106 course outline, which of the following is NOT one of the major topics covered?

options.A: Quantum physics formulas
options.B: History and evolution of drama / origin of drama
options.C: Elements of drama (plot, setting, theme, character, etc.)
options.D: Forms of drama (tragedy, comedy, tragic-comedy)

questions.explanation: The LIT106 course outline covers the definition of drama, its history/origin, components, theories, elements, dramatic techniques, and forms of drama - it does not cover quantum physics formulas.

questions.stem: In drama, what does the term 'Cast' refer to?

options.A: The group of actors and actresses who perform the roles/characters in a play
options.B: The written script of a play before performance
options.C: The location where a play is staged
options.D: The final speech that closes a play

questions.explanation: Cast refers to the group of actors and actresses who perform the roles or characters in a play. It is listed among the other features of drama alongside flashback, suspense, climax, interlude, dramatis personae, and soliloquy.

questions.stem: What does 'Dramatis Personae' mean, and where is it usually found in a play text?

options.A: It is Latin for 'persons of the drama'; it is the list of characters in a play, usually found at the beginning of the play text
options.B: It is the closing speech of a play
options.C: It is a French term meaning 'untying of a knot'
options.D: It refers to the stage setting of a play

questions.explanation: Dramatis Personae is the list of characters in a play, typically presented at the beginning of the play text, identifying who the characters are before the action begins.

questions.stem: What is a 'Soliloquy' in drama?

options.A: A speech in which a character, alone on stage, speaks his or her thoughts aloud to the audience
options.B: A song performed by a chorus of fifty men
options.C: A conversation between two or more characters
options.D: An obstacle placed in the protagonist's way

questions.explanation: A soliloquy is a speech in which a character, usually alone on stage, speaks his or her inner thoughts aloud, allowing the audience direct access to that character's mind without addressing another character.

questions.stem: What is an 'Interlude' in the context of drama?

options.A: A short performance or entertainment piece presented between the acts or scenes of a longer play
options.B: The main climax of a play
options.C: The list of characters in a play
options.D: The struggle between the protagonist and antagonist

questions.explanation: An interlude is a short performance or entertainment piece presented between the acts or scenes of a longer dramatic work, often providing a pause or transition.

questions.stem: How do 'Acts' and 'Scenes' relate to each other and to the whole play?

options.A: A play is made up of acts, and acts are made up of scenes; scenes are complete episodes under an act
options.B: A play is made up of scenes only, and acts do not exist
options.C: An act is a smaller unit found inside a single scene
options.D: Acts and scenes are exactly the same thing with different names

questions.explanation: A play is made up of acts, and acts are made up of scenes. Scenes are the performable parts into which a drama is divided; they are under an act and are complete episodes to be dramatized.

questions.stem: What structure did William Shakespeare make the standard for his plays?

options.A: The five-act structure
options.B: The three-act structure
options.C: The single continuous scene structure
options.D: The ten-act structure

questions.explanation: William Shakespeare made the five-act structure the standard for his plays, unlike poems which are written in stanzas; drama is presented in acts and scenes.

questions.stem: What is the name given to the theory which holds that drama emanated from ritual practices performed to appease the gods?

options.A: The Ritual Origin Theory
options.B: The Mimetic Impulse Theory
options.C: The Alienation Theory
options.D: The Catharsis Theory

questions.explanation: The Ritual Origin Theory holds that drama emanated from ritual; when there was chaos or the land was not yielding fruit, people thought they had offended the gods, and the act of appeasing the gods through a priest's special dress and incantations is what is studied as the Ritual Origin Theory.

questions.stem: Which TWO theories of the origin of drama are covered in this course?

options.A: The Ritual Origin Theory and the Mimetic Impulse Theory
options.B: The Catharsis Theory and the Alienation Theory
options.C: The Classical Theory and the Modern Theory
options.D: The Comedy Theory and the Tragedy Theory

questions.explanation: The two theories of the origin of drama covered are the Ritual Origin Theory (drama emanating from rituals to appease the gods) and the Mimetic Impulse Theory (the imitation of actions).

questions.stem: According to the notes, how many types of characters are there, and what are they called?

options.A: Two types: Flat character and Round character
options.B: Three types: Flat, Round, and Static
options.C: Four types: Protagonist, Antagonist, Flat, and Round
options.D: One type: only the Protagonist

questions.explanation: There are two types of character: Flat character (static, does not change) and Round character (dynamic, grows and develops with the play).

questions.stem: Which component of drama is responsible for keeping the plot moving, distinct from the verbal exchange among characters?

options.A: Action
options.B: Dialogue
options.C: Theme
options.D: Setting

questions.explanation: Action is what keeps the plot moving, as the play emerges from the enactment of action before an audience; this is distinct from Dialogue, which is the verbal exchange among characters.

questions.stem: Which three components together make up the foundation of drama, as introduced at the very start of the course notes?

options.A: Action, Dialogue, and Conflict
options.B: Plot, Theme, and Setting
options.C: Tragedy, Comedy, and Tragic-comedy
options.D: Cast, Dramatis Personae, and Soliloquy

questions.explanation: The notes open by stating that the components of drama are Action, Dialogue, and Conflict, which together form the foundation for understanding how a play functions.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes Conflict from Dialogue as components of drama?

options.A: Conflict is a continuing force that comes from the interaction of characters and is resolved at the end (denouement), while Dialogue is the verbal exchange that releases the playwright's intentions
options.B: Conflict and Dialogue mean exactly the same thing in drama
options.C: Conflict only happens in comedy, while Dialogue only happens in tragedy
options.D: Conflict is a type of costume, while Dialogue is a type of stage setting

questions.explanation: Conflict is a continuing force in a drama which comes naturally out of the interaction of characters and is resolved at the end (denouement), while Dialogue is the verbal exchange among characters which helps release the playwright's intentions (except in Mime).

questions.stem: To which century and place can tragedy be traced, according to the notes?

options.A: Greece, in the 5th century BC
options.B: Rome, in the 1st century AD
options.C: England, in the 16th century AD
options.D: Egypt, in the 3rd century BC

questions.explanation: Tragedy is a dramatic form generally believed to have originated from Greece; it can be traced to Greece of the 5th century BC.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the MOST complete list of the functions of drama given in the notes?

options.A: It entertains, informs and educates; presents a story realistically through actors; is an effective tool for mass mobilization; has an immediate message; forms part of communal rites; and mirrors society to effect social reforms
options.B: It only entertains people with no other social value
options.C: It exists purely for religious worship and has no entertainment value
options.D: It only functions during festivals and has no everyday use

questions.explanation: The functions of drama listed are: (1) it entertains, informs, and educates people, (2) it presents a story in a realistic fashion through the actors to the audience, (3) it is an effective tool for mass mobilization, (4) its message is immediate, (5) it forms part of communal rites, and (6) it mirrors the society and helps to effect social reforms.

questions.stem: What is the key distinguishing feature of drama as a 'Branch of Literature', separating it from prose and poetry?

options.A: Its composition is dramatic, making use of dialogue from beginning to end, with information passed on a stage
options.B: It cannot be written down at all
options.C: It has no characters or plot
options.D: It is only ever performed, never read

questions.explanation: As a branch of literature, drama's composition is dramatic; the major difference between drama and other forms of literature (prose and poetry) is that drama makes use of dialogue from the beginning to the end, and information is passed on a stage.

questions.stem: The word 'drama' is from the Greek verb 'dran'. Which of the following best captures its full implication as discussed in the notes?

options.A: It means 'to act or perform', and many scholars argue this performative root links drama's origin to ritual
options.B: It means 'to write silently', with no connection to performance
options.C: It means 'to dance only', excluding speech entirely
options.D: It means 'to read aloud', excluding any physical movement

questions.explanation: Drama is from the Greek verb 'dran', meaning 'to act or perform'. Many scholars have argued that drama emanated from ritual, connecting the performative root of the word to its ritual origins.

questions.stem: According to the LIT106 course outline, which dramatic techniques are explicitly listed together as a group?

options.A: Suspense, Comic relief, Flashback, Foreshadowing, Dramatic Irony, and Deus Ex Machina
options.B: Plot, Setting, Theme, and Character
options.C: Tragedy, Comedy, and Tragic-comedy
options.D: Exposition, Complication, and Climax

questions.explanation: The course outline groups Suspense, Comic relief, Flashback, Foreshadowing, Dramatic Irony, and Deus Ex Machina together under Dramatic Techniques, separate from Elements of Drama and Forms of Drama.

questions.stem: Which two additional topics appear at the end of the LIT106 course outline, listed separately from 'Forms of Drama'?

options.A: Dramatic Irony and Alienation Effect
options.B: Catharsis and Hubris
options.C: Plot and Setting
options.D: Ritual Origin Theory and Mimetic Impulse Theory

questions.explanation: The course outline lists Dramatic Irony and Alienation Effect as separate bullet points after 'Forms of Drama (Tragedy, Comedy, Tragic-comedy, etc.)', even though Dramatic Irony also appears earlier among the dramatic techniques.

questions.stem: In the classical tradition, elevated language for tragedy is seen as which literary form?

options.A: Verse
options.B: Prose
options.C: Free dialogue with no structure
options.D: Mime with no words

questions.explanation: Elevated language is the ideal language for tragedy in the classical tradition, and this elevated language is seen as verse.

questions.stem: How do 'Deus Ex Machina' and 'Alienation Effect' differ from one another?

options.A: Deus Ex Machina brings a supernatural force on stage to solve a problem, while Alienation Effect is a detachment injected by directors to prevent emotional involvement
options.B: Both terms mean exactly the same thing
options.C: Deus Ex Machina is about audience emotion, while Alienation Effect is about solving plot problems
options.D: Neither term has anything to do with directors or supernatural forces

questions.explanation: Deus Ex Machina means bringing in a supernatural force (a god) to the stage to solve a problem, while Alienation Effect is a detachment injected by directors into the way actors and audience relate with their plays, to prevent too much emotional involvement.

questions.stem: Which term means 'actors or characters impersonating specific characters in the main action'?

options.A: Re-enactment
options.B: Re-presentation
options.C: Imitation
options.D: Catharsis

questions.explanation: Re-enactment refers to actors or characters who impersonate specific characters in the main action, while re-presentation refers simply to showing something again.
